title: New license request: Space Child License v1.0
body:
### How license meets inclusion principles

The Space Child License is a permissive licence carrying a use restriction (a "Peace Clause"). It grants broad, royalty-free rights for peaceful use and withdraws them for seven enumerated harms: armed aggression, civilian-targeting weapons systems, autonomous lethal decision-making, mass surveillance for persecution, suppression of expression and assembly, severe environmental destruction, and forced labour or trafficking.

**Against the definitive factors**

**A. Does not match an existing entry.** Nothing currently on the list pairs a permissive grant with this clause set. The nearest relatives are `Hippocratic-2.1` and `Hippocratic-3.0-core`, and the difference is structural rather than cosmetic: those incorporate external human-rights standards wholesale, whereas this licence enumerates specific prohibited uses inline and then, in section 8.6, names the instruments those terms are to be read against.

**B. Not OSI-approved, and not submitted to OSI.** Stated plainly rather than left to be discovered: a field-of-use restriction is incompatible with OSD §6 and with FSF freedom 0, so this licence is not open source under either definition and is not presented as one. The project README says so in those words, so that nobody adopts it expecting otherwise.

**C. Applies to source code, not only executables.** Section 3 conditions redistribution on retaining notices and does not restrict source availability.

**D. The text is identifiable and stable.** v1.0 is final and not in drafting. It is byte-identical across all 37 adopting repositories — 14,714 bytes, `sha256 bb4b0941a67dcd6c…` — verified by hashing the file independently in five of them before writing this.

**E. Versioning commitment.** The steward commits to not modifying the v1.0 text after addition to the list. Any future change will ship as a new version with its own number and its own file. This is published as policy in the canonical repository rather than only asserted here.

**Against the other factors**

**1 / 4.** The licence does not meet an OSI or FSF definition, so factor 4 is the applicable route: it is primarily intended for the free distribution of source code with limited restrictions. The restrictions are a closed list of seven, each tied to an existing international instrument rather than to the licensor's discretion, and they bind *conduct* rather than field of commerce — commercial use, modification, redistribution and private use are all unconditionally permitted.

**2. Structured to be generally usable by anyone.** The operative text contains no reference to any project, product, organization or person. A single attribution line in the closing footer names the authors; it imposes no obligation and does not scope the grant. Any third party can adopt the text unchanged.

**3. Actual use.** 37 repositories, 24 of them public, spanning an industrial-control platform, an operating-system kernel, a Rust agent runtime and the libraries beneath them.

Stated candidly, because it is the weakest point of this submission: **that use is concentrated in a single organization.** The licence has not yet been adopted outside `kannaka-labs`. We are submitting now precisely because the absence of an identifier is what blocks wider adoption — registries and scanners resolve it as `NOASSERTION` and deny by default, which is operationally identical to carrying no licence at all. We would rather have that weighed openly than found.

**5.** The steward is the submitter and supports this submission.

If the Legal Team concludes that adoption is currently too narrow, we would welcome that answer stated as such, so we can return when the evidence is stronger rather than re-litigate it now.

B) **Not OSI-approved, but not required**: CCBL has not been submitted to OSI. This factor permits automatic inclusion for OSI licenses, but does not require OSI approval.

C) **Source code available**: CCBL §2.1 requires that anyone distributing the software must also provide the complete source code. This is not an executable-only license.

D) **Stable, finalized text**: CCBL 1.7 has undergone five rounds of legal review and is published as a finalized version. The text is not in draft or pre-release status. It is available at https://github.com/ccbl-license/ccbl-license/blob/main/LICENSE and archived in the /versions/ directory with both .txt (authoritative) and .md formats.

E) **Versioning commitment**: The license steward (Ignotus Labs) maintains a numbered version archive (1.6 → 1.7) and will not modify published versions. New versions receive new version numbers and are published alongside prior versions.

1) **Does not substantially conform to an Open Source Definition**: CCBL intentionally restricts commercial use (§3) and AI training/provision (Appendix A §5). **4.** Comments: While the license is new and therefore has not found wide adoption yet, we encountered following problem compelling us to create a new license: 
The current license landscape does not provide lightweight license for unrestricted usage by end users but restriction on distribution by software as a service providers such as cloud hosting services. For this purpose the BSD license has been extended containing additional conditions.  

**Where it differs from existing 4 Clause BSD Licenses:** 
While this license provides general availability of source code and no restrictions in usage for personal and commercial use by end users, it restricts the commercial viability of the source code for resellers of the source code (for example offering the source code as a, service offering in cloud), also as combiled binary in any form (such as HTML representations). 

The current license options with such restrictions are either very long (eg Affero License) or proprietary (such as the redis license,  [https://redis.io/legal/licenses/](https://redis.io/legal/licenses/)). 

We are trying to solve these issues by providing a license that: 
- is (non-legal) human readable
- is easy to understand 
- allows unrestricted end user ownership of the code
- prohibits redistribution as paid service without added value
- allows modifications

OSI approval given the restrictions was neither desired nor possible as OSI does not allow posing such restrictions.

The license itself comes inside a github repository with: 
- Full explanation (https://github.com/gms-electronics/GMS-License/);
- A matrix to understand better what can or can't be done with it;
- A full markdown template; 
- A full XML representation. 

While we are aware that this license stretches the admissibility standards, we hope you can get on board with us given that exclusions became more prevalent over the past years and a more digestable license

I'd like the DevWheels Licence to be considered for listing. This is a licence that I wrote and steward, and which I use on three of my software packages.

I've read the inclusion principles, and although the licence meets all SPDX's definitive factors, the licence doesn't fully comply with either the OSI or FSF criteria, and I'm not sure how "substantially complies" is interpreted. The main features of the DevWheels licence are:

2. If released, buildable source of the entire package must be made available,

6. The cost of an upgrade is by default the price difference between the two versions, and
7. Run licences can be transferred and sold.

It's basically AGPL with a monetary restriction on Freedom Zero if deployed. That is, preserving full freedom to tinker and share, but transferring some freedom that many users ([and licence-writers](https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/selling.html)) consider less important to aid each developer in a fair way.
